lead: Proof of Work is the rule that makes a block expensive to produce. A miner searches for a nonce so that SHA-256 applied twice to the 80-byte header, read as a 256-bit number, falls below a target. Bitcoin double-hashes; some other chains hash once. Finding a winning hash takes many tries, checking it takes one. The target is retuned so blocks arrive steadily. Building blocks and hunting the winning hash is called mining.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 for SHA-256 and the block header, and 3.3 for where proof of work sits among the consensus types.

sections.h3: The puzzle in the block header

blocks.text: A miner fills a candidate block: transactions from the mempool, and a coinbase line that pays the miner's own address the block reward plus fees (see 3.2). Then it hashes only the block header, 80 bytes long, with six fields: version, previous block hash, Merkle root of the transactions, timestamp, target bits, and nonce.

The target bits field encodes the target T, a 256-bit number. Bitcoin accepts the block only if SHA-256(SHA-256(header)), read as an integer, is less than T. Single SHA-256 is used by some other chains, not by Bitcoin. A small T leaves very few winning outputs out of the 2²⁵⁶ possible hashes, so the puzzle is costly to solve and cheap to check.
p = T ÷ 2²⁵⁶ ≈ 16⁻ᶻ   and   expected tries = 1 ÷ p = 16ᶻ
blocks.where: p is the probability that one hash attempt wins; z is the number of leading zero hexadecimal digits the target demands; 16ᶻ is sixteen raised to the power z.

items: Assemble the candidate block and its coinbase transaction.
Compute the Merkle root of the transactions and write the header.
Hash the header with SHA-256 twice (SHA-256d) and compare the result, as an integer, with T.
If the hash is below T, broadcast the block and collect the reward.
Otherwise add 1 to the nonce and hash again.
If the 32-bit nonce wraps around, change the timestamp or an extra nonce inside the coinbase and keep going.

blocks.text: Difficulty D is a rescaled way of stating the target: D = T₁ ÷ T, where T₁ is the target of difficulty 1, the fixed value 0x00000000FFFF0000 followed by zeros, and T is the target in use. A higher difficulty means a smaller target and more expected hashes per block. Difficulty is not a hash rate; it says how hard the puzzle is, not how fast anyone runs.
Bitcoin aims at one block per 10 minutes. Every 2016 blocks (about two weeks) each node recomputes the difficulty from the time the window actually took.
D_new = D_old × (2016 × 10 min) ÷ actual time for the window
blocks.where: D_old and D_new are the difficulty before and after the retune; 2016 × 10 min = 20160 min = 14 days is the target duration; actual time is measured from the timestamps of the first and last block of the window.

blocks.text: If the window finished in 12 days, blocks came too fast, so difficulty rises by 14 ÷ 12. If it took 16 days, difficulty falls by 14 ÷ 16. Bitcoin limits one adjustment to a factor of 4 up or down, so a timestamp error cannot jump the difficulty wildly.

items: CPU: the first miners used ordinary processors, a few million hashes per second.
GPU: graphics cards run thousands of simple lanes in parallel, giving a large jump.
FPGA: field-programmable chips wire the hash function directly and waste less power.
ASIC: application-specific chips do only SHA-256, nothing else, and dominate today.

blocks.text: As ASICs pushed the network hash rate up, a single machine almost never finds a block alone. Miners join a pool. The pool manager builds the candidate block, hands each member a different template, and counts shares: any hash that falls below the pool's easy share target. A share measures effort. If a share also falls below the network target, it is the block solution as well as a share, and the pool submits it and splits the reward.

Payment schemes differ. Pay-per-share pays a fixed amount for every valid share, so the miner has steady income and the pool carries the luck. Proportional schemes pay only when the pool finds a block, in proportion to shares. Pool hopping was an early exploit: miners joined a pool near the end of a round, when expected payout per share was high, and left at the reset. Score-based or pay-per-share accounting now blunts it.

The security claim is that rewriting history costs as much as writing it. An attacker with more than half the hash rate can mine a private chain faster than the honest network and publish it later, replacing recent blocks. That allows double spending: pay in a transaction on the public chain, then release a longer private chain without it. The same power can censor transactions. It cannot forge signatures, so it cannot spend coins that belong to someone else.
Selfish mining is a subtler strategy: a pool withholds blocks and releases them at chosen moments to waste rivals' work. Only the name is needed here.

The cost is real electricity. Energy use is roughly hash rate × joules per hash; ASICs lowered joules per hash, but the total climbed as hash rate grew. Mining also produces electronic waste when rigs are replaced. Chains that dislike this cost move to 3.5 or to fair-turn rules such as 3.6.

figure.caption: Four leading zero hex digits happen once in 16⁴ = 65,536 tries. When 2016 blocks take 12 days instead of 14, the next difficulty is the old one × 14/12 ≈ 1.1667, a rise of about 16.67%.

examples.question: A target requires the first four hex digits of the 256-bit block hash to be zero. (a) Find the probability that one hash attempt succeeds and the expected number of tries. (b) A miner runs at 2 × 10¹¹ hashes per second; how long would it take on average if it owned the whole network's hash rate? (c) A difficulty window of 2016 blocks finishes in 12 days instead of the target 14 days. Find the new difficulty and the percentage change.
steps: One hex digit has 16 possible values, so the chance that a given digit is zero is 1/16. For z = 4 independent digits: p = (1/16)⁴ = 1/16⁴ = 1/65536 ≈ 1.526 × 10⁻⁵.
Time = tries ÷ hash rate = 65536 ÷ (2 × 10¹¹ hashes per second) = 3.2768 × 10⁻⁷ s.
Target window duration = 2016 blocks × 10 min per block = 20160 min = 14 days. Actual duration = 12 days = 17280 min.
New difficulty = old difficulty × (20160 ÷ 17280) = old difficulty × 1.1667.
examples.answer: Expected tries = 65536 hashes at p ≈ 1.526 × 10⁻⁵, the run takes 3.2768 × 10⁻⁷ s at 2 × 10¹¹ hashes per second, and the difficulty rises by a factor of 1.1667, that is by about 16.67%.
examples.check:
z = 4
p = 1 / 16**z
tries = 1 / p
hash_rate = 2e11
t = tries / hash_rate
target_min = 2016 * 10
actual_min = 12 * 24 * 60
factor = target_min / actual_min
print(int(round(tries)))
print(round(t, 12))
print(round(factor, 4))
print(round((factor - 1) * 100, 2))

traps: Thinking more leading zeros make mining easier. More zeros means a smaller target, so fewer hashes win and mining is harder.
Confusing difficulty with hash rate. Difficulty fixes the puzzle; hash rate is how fast a machine tries. Rising hash rate forces difficulty upward at the next retune.
Comparing the hash as a string of zeros instead of as a 256-bit integer below a target. Two hashes with the same leading zeros can fall on opposite sides of T.
Using 2016 × 10 seconds instead of 2016 × 10 minutes for the window. The target window is 14 days, not about 5.6 hours.
Claiming a 51% attacker can steal coins. It can reorder and censor, and double spend its own coins, but it cannot forge signatures or spend other people's coins.

quiz.q: Which field of the block header does a miner change while searching for a winning hash?
quiz.a: The nonce, a 32-bit counter. When it wraps around, the miner also varies the timestamp or an extra nonce in the coinbase.

quiz.q: State the difficulty definition and the retune formula.
quiz.a: D = T₁ ÷ T, where T₁ is the target of difficulty 1 and T is the current target. Every 2016 blocks, D_new = D_old × (2016 × 10 min) ÷ actual window time.

quiz.q: Why is proof of work cheap for other nodes to check even though it is costly to produce?
quiz.a: A node hashes the header twice with SHA-256 and compares the result with T. The miner may need 16ᶻ tries, but the checker needs one double hash, so verification cost does not grow with difficulty.

quiz.q: Why does difficulty have to rise when the network hash rate rises?
quiz.a: With faster hashing, the same target would be beaten more often and blocks would arrive faster than one per 10 minutes. The window would finish early, so the retune multiplies difficulty by target time ÷ actual time, restoring the 10-minute spacing.

quiz.q: A target demands five leading zero hex digits. Find the probability per try and the expected number of tries.
A 2016-block window takes 16 days. The old difficulty is 8000. Find the new difficulty (respect the factor-of-4 clamp).
quiz.a: Target time = 14 days, actual = 16 days, ratio = 14/16 = 0.875. New difficulty = 8000 × 0.875 = 7000. The change is a fall by a factor of 0.875, well inside the clamp, so it stands.

quiz.q: A miner with 1% of the network hash rate mines solo. Explain why joining a pool changes the variance of its income but not its expected income, ignoring pool fees.
quiz.a: Expected income per unit time equals hash rate share × total reward, whether solo or pooled. Solo mining pays a whole block rarely, so the variance is huge and income is bursty. In a pool the same expected income arrives as many small share payments, so variance falls sharply. Pay-per-share changes who carries the luck (the pool, not the miner), not the underlying expected reward; only pool fees and default or orphan risk can shift expected value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real mining is an industrial business: ASIC fabs, cheap power contracts and immersion cooling decide who survives, and difficulty becomes a public measure of that competition. Research has moved toward memory-hard puzzles that resist ASICs, and toward proofs that reuse work, such as proof of useful work. Verifiable delay functions are a separate primitive: they force a fixed delay, not useful work. Some newer designs also replace the winner-takes-all race with weighted lotteries, which is the bridge to proof of stake. Search for memory-hard proof of work, ASIC resistance, selfish mining, and self-contained proofs of work.
